newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico opposition senator says doubts trade data.
newsitem.headline: Mexico opposition senator says doubts trade data.

text.p: A senator for the opposition National Action Party (PAN) on Monday released a letter he sent to Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz, saying Mexico had dangerously inflated the size of the country's trade surplus by including figures from the maquiladora, or in-bond, industry.

Though he acknowledged that maquiladora imports and exports are included in the trade data for statistical purposes, Sen. Jose Angel Conchello said their inclusion was helping foster a boom in imports by what he termed the "charming bourgeoisie."

On Jan. 23, Mexico reported a 1996 trade surplus of $6.292 billion, made up of exports of $95.929 billion, including maquiladora sales abroad, and imports of $89.637 billion, including in-bond imports.
But Conchello said maquiladora imports were $31 billion while exports from the assembly plants were $37 billion.

He said the maquiladora figures -- which count components imported duty free, assembled and then re-exported in free-trade zones -- did not represent a real gain for the economy, and only benefited the books of the multi-national companies that own them.
Excluding maquiladora data, the trade surplus would have been a wafer-thin $200 million, he said. Without oil exports, he said, it would have become a deficit of more than $10 billion.

"If the public knew that eliminating temporary maquiladora trade and taking away crude oil, we had a national economic deficit of more than $10 billion in 1996, there would be many who instead of buying imported wood for their fireplaces, or foreign food for their pets, could begin to buy made-in-Mexico goods," the letter said.

He said the import boom ran the risk of leading to a repeat of the crisis that caused the 1994 peso devaluation. He pointed out with praise that in South Korea, for example, "patriotic burning" of imported goods is encouraged.
